beats.narration_text: Hi — I'm Divij Pawar. This is part two of When Two Agents Disagree. Last time: correctness needs ground truth, disagreement needs nothing, and the safe move is to surface a conflict rather than resolve it. This time I'll show you what I actually built on top of that — three files, twenty-one tests, and nothing else in the system changed.

props.command: What does cross-agent validation look like when you actually build it?
output: Three new files. Everything else in the layer, unchanged.
The comparison itself is one line of set arithmetic.
A flagged contradiction is recorded, never resolved.

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole thing in one breath. I already had an accountability layer that made an agent's reasoning permanently on the record — but it could only prove what was said, never whether it was true. Cross-agent validation was already on the architecture diagram: specified, named, and completely empty. So I built the smallest honest version. Run two agents, compare their numbers, write down where they disagree, and stop. No judge. No model. Set arithmetic.

shot.concept: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW. One card, no code, no data. An immaculate stack of timestamped records builds up — crisp, orderly, obviously well-engineered — then the whole stack desaturates under the caption PERFECT RECORD. UNKNOWN TRUTH. A second, empty slot labelled CROSS-AGENT VALIDATION sits beside it and fills with a single terracotta line. Names the shape and the stakes; spends none of the reveals (no symmetric difference, no mutation table, no orphan counters).

beats.narration_text: Four things already existed. The ReasoningObject — one frozen record per agent attempt, holding the conclusion, the steps, the confidence, the sources. The validation loop — output must parse into a required structure, one retry, then halt; both attempts get recorded either way, because a failed attempt is evidence too. The store — SQLite, with database-level triggers that abort any update or delete, so you cannot quietly edit history. And the consistency probe, which already had the scoring: sixty percent number overlap, forty percent word overlap, three thresholds. All of that existed. It was just pointed at one agent, compared against a repeat of itself.

shot.concept: A four-part component diagram; each part lights in turn, then all four stay lit as a single system. Part 2 (the validation loop) gets a small inset flow: ATTEMPT 1 - parse? - SUCCESS, else ATTEMPT 2 - SUCCESS or HALT, with both attempts dropping records into the same stack. Part 3 shows a RAISE(ABORT) stamp on an attempted edit. Part 4 shows the 0.6 / 0.4 weights and the three thresholds in PT Mono (data job). Do NOT set 'ReasoningObject' through an uppercase chip helper - it smashes to 'REASONINGOBJECT' with no visible break (tips.txt section 9). Write it as 'Reasoning Object' or keep mixed case.

beats.narration_text: So I audited the project to find where this could actually be useful, and the answer was already on the published architecture diagram. The orchestration layer declared three mechanisms: cross-agent validation, dynamic task allocation, pattern recognition. All three had zero implementation. But cross-agent validation was the best-specified orphan in the repo — twenty-one thousand, eight hundred and twenty-four bytes of specification, sixteen scaffolded scripts, and zero shared logic connecting them. That's the pattern everywhere. The node layer is thirty thousand, four hundred and ninety-seven lines; one thousand two hundred and seventy-six of those are real logic. Tests: zero. And why had nobody built it? Cross-agent validation needs two agents that emit comparable conclusions. The project had approximately zero.

shot.concept: Three movements. (1) The published architecture diagram draws in — four agent categories, an orchestration layer on top holding three named mechanisms. All three stamp ZERO IMPLEMENTATION; the spotlight lands on CROSS-AGENT VALIDATION. (2) A counter panel ticks up in PT Mono: 21,824 bytes / 1 conductor doc / 16 scripts / 0 shared logic. The last row is the punchline — let it land alone. (3) Two bars: 30,497 total vs 1,276 real logic. The gap is the story, so give the small bar a label and let the empty space carry the rest. tips.txt section 6: three mechanism nodes with chips underneath collided in the last reel - wrap 'Dynamic Task Allocation' and 'Pattern Recognition' to two lines.

beats.narration_text: Version one got scoped down until it was almost boring, and the cuts are the design. Producer A: a real agent, already wired to live SEC EDGAR endpoints. Producer B: a hand-written fixture that returns a conclusion I pick in advance. That sounds like cheating. It isn't. If both producers are real and the comparator says contradiction, you can't tell whether they genuinely disagree or your comparator is broken. With a fixture, a wrong result can only be the comparator's fault. Second cut: contradiction means numeric divergence only. No entailment model, no judge. Third cut: it writes a record and stops — no escalation, no alert. And no new HTTP route: the layer has four open critical security findings, and adding no route adds no new exposure.

shot.concept: Two boxes first: AgentID.FINANCIAL wired to a live EDGAR endpoint, and AgentID.EARNINGS wired to a hand-written fixture. Then the fixture justification, done visually rather than narrated: two hypotheses branch off a CONTRADICTION node - 'they disagree' / 'comparator broken' - and with two real producers neither branch can be eliminated; the fixture kills one branch and the surviving branch highlights. Ends on a checklist: five items checked IN SCOPE, seven struck through DEFERRED, each deferred item carrying a one-word reason. Use checked() from graphics_lib for the ticks - never put a check glyph inside a font-forced Text() (tips.txt section 4). Twelve checklist rows at floor type size will run past y = -3.6; compress the row spacing and check the LAST row's position before rendering 4K (tips.txt section 7).

beats.narration_text: Three files, and the test file is the biggest of them — that ratio isn't an accident. Each agent gets its own context: information asymmetry, encoded in a function signature. When an agent fails validation twice, the loop raises, and its records get carried forward rather than dropped, because a halt is a fact somebody may want to see. Then the comparison, in full: extract the numbers from both conclusions, take the symmetric difference, and anything in exactly one of them is a divergence. No model. No judge. Set arithmetic. The scoring wasn't rewritten, it was re-pointed — same weights, same thresholds, imported unmodified. And one line covers both cases: a different value is caught, and a missing number is caught by the same rule.

shot.concept: The visual spine of the video - give the symmetric-difference animation the most screen time in the reel. (1) File tree: three items marked NEW, six marked UNCHANGED; the test file is visibly the largest. (2) The halt handler as real source on a PT Mono card, held long enough to read - four lines, no more. (3) The set animation: two number sets fill from two conclusions, the intersection cancels out, and what remains in exactly one set lifts out in terracotta. Run it twice - once for 12% vs 8%, once for 12% vs nothing - so 'same rule, no special case' is shown, not stated. Real source text only, PT Mono, never prose restyled as code.

beats.act: how it fits, and proving the tests can fail
beats.narration_text: Now, how it lives inside the layer rather than beside it. Both agents share one run ID, because here the comparison is the evidence — flag a contradiction without producing both conclusions and you've published an accusation with no exhibits. The runs table stores a free-form JSON blob, so a whole new kind of record needed no migration and no new column. One new key. And it inherits the append-only triggers for free: once a flag is written, it can't be updated or deleted. Then, the tests. Twenty-one new, all passing — which is worth almost nothing. A passing suite proves your tests agree with your code, not that they'd notice if the code were wrong. So I broke it on purpose. Swap the symmetric difference for an intersection: seven tests fail. Return false instead of null when no comparison happened: three more.

SECOND HALF: a big green 129/129, then a question mark beside it; then the mutation table builds row by row. Close on the false-vs-null two-chip comparison - that is the sharpest idea in the reel, so it gets the last four seconds and no competing motion. beats.narration_text: So let's be precise about what this is not. Comparison is numeric only — two conclusions that disagree completely while citing the same figures sail straight through. Producer B is still a fixture, so no genuine disagreement has ever been observed on live data. It isn't SQL-queryable. And a flagged contradiction triggers nothing.

props.artifactHeading: What version one does not do
artifactLines: Numeric divergence only - two conclusions can disagree in prose and still pass.
Producer B is a fixture; no real cross-agent disagreement observed on live data.
Stored in a JSON blob: retrievable by run ID, not queryable in SQL.
A flagged contradiction triggers nothing. No alert. No escalation. No named human.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: "Find one place in my system where a check returns false when it actually means the check could not run." That's the null-versus-false distinction, aimed at your own code. False claims a check happened and came back clean. Null says the check couldn't run. A system that silently converts the second into the first manufactures an all-clear out of a failure. Go find one.
